title: Instrument loans
brief: Prepare a decision paper for a city youth orchestra revising its instrument loan program. There are 75 instruments, 62 out on loan, 14 applicants waiting, and 9 instruments due for repair. Sibling sharing is allowed and poorly recorded. Last term 6 instruments returned late; 4 families had outdated contact details. Average repair bill 90 currency units. A sponsor offers 3,000 for one year but bars spending on deposits. Teachers disagree over refundable deposits versus a no-deposit trial. Rehearsals start in six weeks. Write for a board including parents and finance volunteers. Distinguish choices that affect access from choices that affect recovery and repair.

5480eea5cdb05595.text:
# Instrument Loan Program: Decision Paper for the Board

## Decision sought

The board is asked to settle the loan terms for the coming year before rehearsals start in six weeks. The recommendation is to:

1. Run a one-year no-deposit trial with pass/fail tests agreed now.
2. Adopt a set of recovery measures that apply whichever way the deposit question goes.
3. Accept the sponsor's 3,000 and commit 810 of it at once to the nine outstanding repairs.
4. Allocate available instruments to the waiting list by a published rule.

The paper separates two kinds of choice. **Access choices** decide which children get an instrument. **Recovery and repair choices** decide whether instruments come back on time and in playable condition. Most of the recovery measures can be tightened without affecting access. The deposit is the exception, which is why it divides the teachers.

## Where we stand

| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| Instruments owned | 75 |
| Out on loan | 62 |
| Not on loan | 13 |
| Due for repair | 9 |
| Applicants waiting | 14 |
| Late returns last term | 6 |
| Families with outdated contact details | 4 |
| Average repair bill | 90 |
| Cost of the nine repairs at the average | 810 |
| Sponsor offer (one year, not for deposits) | 3,000 |
| Sponsor money left after the nine repairs | 2,190 |

## What we do not yet know

Four gaps limit how firm any decision can be, and all can be closed in the first two weeks.

- **Where the nine repair instruments are.** If all nine are among the 13 not on loan, only four instruments are ready to issue today. If some are in players' hands, more are ready now, but those players will need cover while their instruments are repaired.
- **Whether the stock matches the demand.** Thirteen instruments for 14 applicants looks like a shortfall of one, but the real gap depends on type and size, and a spare cello does not help a waiting flautist.
- **How many children the 62 loans serve.** Because sibling sharing is poorly recorded, we do not know how many players depend on loaned instruments or which adult is responsible for each one.
- **Whether the late returns and the outdated contacts are the same families.** If they largely overlap, the main cause of late returns is that we could not reach people, which a deposit would not fix.

## Choices that affect access

### 1. Who gets the available instruments

Even after every repair, there are at most 13 instruments for 14 applicants, so at least one applicant will wait. The board should set the rule before names are attached to it. The recommended order is:

1. Applicants for whom a suitable instrument (type and size) is available.
2. Among those, children with no other access to an instrument.
3. Then date of application.

The rule and each applicant's position should be shared with families, so that those still waiting know why.

### 2. Sibling sharing

Sharing widens access because one instrument serves two children. The recommendation is to keep it but record it. Each loan should name every child who plays the instrument and one adult responsible for it.

Recording will also show whether any siblings are expected to play the same instrument in the same rehearsal. Those cases are unmet demand that the waiting list does not currently show.

### 3. Review of long-held loans

Some of the 62 loans may be instruments a child has outgrown or no longer plays. An annual confirmation that each instrument is still the right size and in regular use costs nothing and may free stock for the waiting list. This should be presented as a check on fit, with no threat of withdrawal.

## Choices that affect recovery and repair

These measures apply under either deposit option, and none of them makes it harder for a child to get an instrument.

- **Contact details confirmed each term.** No instrument is issued or renewed without a confirmed phone number, address, and second contact. This is aimed directly at the four families we could not reach.
- **A signed loan agreement with a fixed return date.** It should take up one page and state the return date, who is responsible, what counts as normal wear, and what happens if the instrument is damaged or late.
- **Reminders before the due date.** Reminders go out two weeks and then two days before the return date, with a named person assigned to follow up.
- **Condition check at issue and return.** A teacher fills in a short checklist with the family present. Without it, we cannot tell wear from damage and cannot have a fair conversation about repair costs.
- **A single register.** One list holds each instrument's identifying number, condition, borrower, sharers, responsible adult, and return date, and one volunteer is responsible for keeping it.
- **Repairs done before reissue.** No instrument should go out in a condition that leads to a bigger bill later.

## The deposit question

The deposit is the one choice that sits in both categories. It is meant as a recovery tool, but it changes who applies.

### The case for refundable deposits

A deposit gives families a financial reason to return instruments on time and in good condition. It also provides money to draw on when an instrument comes back damaged. The teachers who favour it are responding to a real problem, since six late returns in one term is too many.

### The case against deposits

- **The evidence points elsewhere.** The six instruments came back late, but they did come back. Four families could not be reached. That pattern suggests a record-keeping problem more than a lack of incentive.
- **A deposit is a barrier.** Some of the 14 waiting families may not be able to pay one, and families already in the program may hand instruments back to avoid paying. The program exists for the children who cannot buy their own.
- **The sponsor money cannot soften it.** The sponsor bars spending on deposits, so we cannot use the grant to cover deposits for families who cannot pay. Any waiver would simply mean an instrument with no deposit behind it. That creates a two-tier system and requires someone to judge hardship.
- **It adds finance work.** Deposits are other people's money and would have to be held as a liability, not income. Each deposit must be tracked per family, kept separate from operating funds, and refunded promptly. Someone must also decide when a deposit is forfeited, and those decisions will be disputed. No deposit amount has been proposed. One large enough to cover an average repair would be about 90.
- **The timing is poor.** Collecting deposits from up to 62 existing borrowers and 13 new ones in six weeks, alongside repairs and allocation, is a heavy load for volunteers.

### Recommendation: a no-deposit trial with agreed tests

The board should run the coming year without deposits, with all the recovery measures above in place, and agree now what would count as failure. That gives both groups of teachers a fair test and replaces the current disagreement with evidence.

The proposed tests, which the board should adjust as it sees fit, are:

| Measure | Proposed threshold |
|---|---|
| Late returns per term | No more than 3 (half of last term's figure) |
| Instruments unaccounted for at year end | None |
| Loans with confirmed contact details | All |
| Repairs caused by damage, as opposed to wear | Recorded each term, to set a baseline |

If the trial misses the late-return or unaccounted-for tests despite the recovery measures, the board should introduce a deposit the following year. By then it will know how large the deposit needs to be and how many families would need a waiver.

If the board prefers deposits now, the workable version has four features. The amount is modest. The waiver is decided by one named person, privately, against written criteria. The money is held in a separately tracked account. Existing borrowers are phased in over a term so that they are not charged at once.

## Using the sponsor's 3,000

The offer should be accepted. Before the board relies on it, it should confirm in writing with the sponsor that repairs, record-keeping costs, and a held repair reserve are permitted uses, and that the deposit restriction means what we take it to mean.

Because the money is for one year only, it should pay for one-off costs and should not fund anything the orchestra cannot sustain afterwards.

| Use | Amount | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Nine outstanding repairs | 810 | At the average bill; individual repairs will vary |
| In-year repair reserve | 1,000 | Covers about 11 further average repairs |
| Register, instrument tags, cases, and consumables | Up to 400 | To be costed after the audit |
| Unallocated | 790 | Held until the audit shows the real gaps |

The unallocated sum should stay unspent until we know what the waiting list needs. It may go toward an instrument of a type we are short of, or toward repairs that exceed the average. Since 90 is an average, one costly repair could absorb several times that amount.

Finance volunteers should also note what happens after the year ends. If nine instruments need repair in a typical cycle, the program has a recurring cost of roughly 800 a year with no identified funding once the sponsorship lapses. The year-end review should address that alongside the deposit question.

## Timetable

| Week | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Board decision. Sponsor terms confirmed. Repairer asked for turnaround times. |
| 1–2 | Audit of all 75 instruments: location, condition, borrower, sharers. Contact details confirmed for all current borrowers. |
| 2 | Repair instruments sent out, with those matching waiting-list needs sent first. |
| 2–3 | Loan agreement and condition checklist finalised. Register set up. |
| 3–4 | Waiting list matched to stock under the published rule. Families told their position. |
| 4–5 | Repaired instruments returned. Instruments issued with signed agreements. |
| 6 | Rehearsals begin. |

The main risk to this timetable is repair turnaround, which we have not yet confirmed. If repairs cannot be finished in time, the instruments needed by waiting applicants should be repaired first. Any child whose instrument is away for repair should be told before the first rehearsal.

## Decisions for the board

1. Approve a one-year no-deposit trial with the tests above, or direct that a deposit scheme be drawn up.
2. Adopt the recovery measures for all loans, new and existing.
3. Keep sibling sharing, with every sharer and one responsible adult recorded.
4. Approve the waiting-list priority rule.
5. Accept the sponsorship, subject to written confirmation of permitted uses, and approve the allocation.
6. Name one person responsible for the register and one for sponsor reporting.
7. Set a date for the year-end review of the trial and of repair funding after the sponsorship ends.

# Decision paper | Instrument loans for the coming season

## Decision requested

Approve a one-year no-deposit trial, a six-week preparation plan, and a review after the first term. Authorize the loan coordinator to allocate playable instruments under the access rules below. Ask teachers to identify teaching needs and acceptable instrument substitutions, and ask the treasurer to oversee repair spending. Subject to written confirmation of eligible costs, accept the sponsor’s offer of 3,000 currency units for one year. The sponsor bars spending on deposits.

The recommendation rests on two judgments. First, a refundable deposit requires a family to find cash before a player can take an instrument home. Second, the orchestra has practical ways to improve returns and arrange repairs whichever deposit policy it chooses. A trial lets the board test whether those measures are sufficient while keeping entry open to families who would struggle to pay upfront. The board should retain the option to reconsider deposits after it has evidence about missed returns, their causes, and their cost.

## What can be promised before rehearsals

Of 75 instruments, 62 are recorded as out on loan. That leaves 13 outside recorded loans, against 14 applicants waiting. Even if all 13 are playable, suitable, and available, there is one fewer instrument than waiting applicants if each needs a separate loan. Instrument type and size matter. A spare full-size violin does little for a child who needs a quarter-size instrument.

Nine instruments are due for repair. The figures do not show how many of those nine are among the 13, how many are still with borrowers, or which can safely be played until their scheduled repair. If all nine are among the 13 and must be withdrawn immediately, only four would be available before repairs, assuming the other four are playable. If some are with borrowers, repairs could interrupt current players’ access. Sibling sharing adds another uncertainty because the number of instruments on loan does not establish the number of children already served.

The first commitment to families should therefore be a date for an individual update. A place on the waiting list should become a confirmed offer only when the coordinator has identified a suitable instrument, checked its condition, and established a handover date.

## Access decisions

**Upfront payment.** A refundable deposit gives a family a financial reason to complete a return and may reassure volunteers who worry about unrecovered instruments. Its practical value depends on the amount, the refund timetable, and the circumstances in which the orchestra could retain it. A deposit also ties up household cash for the duration of the loan. A waiver could preserve access, although it would require families to know it exists and feel comfortable asking for it. Finance volunteers would have to record each payment as money owed back to the family, reconcile balances, and handle disputed deductions. Sponsor funds cannot pay or underwrite deposits.

The six late returns last term give the board a reason to improve recovery. They do not establish how long families were late, whether another player missed a rehearsal, or whether a deposit would have changed the outcome. The four families with outdated contact details may overlap with the late returns, but the extent of any overlap is unknown. On this evidence, the board has a stronger basis for fixing contact and return arrangements than for setting a particular deposit amount.

**Who receives the next suitable instrument.** Apply one published rule to new applications and renewals. Give priority to a player who would otherwise be unable to participate because they lack regular access to a suitable instrument. Accept a short statement from the family. Among players with equal need for the same type and size, use the date of the original request. Where dates are missing or tied, use a documented draw. Give current borrowers enough notice to plan for a return if their loan will end. Invite families to flag an incorrect size, date, or access assessment before handover.

**When siblings can share.** Keep sharing voluntary. Ask whether both children can practise and attend their scheduled sessions with one instrument and whether the size and setup suit both. If sharing works, list both players under the same instrument number, name one adult contact, and agree one return date. If schedules clash or the instrument fits only one child, assess the second child under the ordinary allocation rule. A household should be able to explain that sharing has stopped working without losing its existing place in the queue. Record each child served so the board can see what sharing actually achieves.

## Recovery decisions

**Make each loan traceable.** Use a single register with an entry for each instrument, including its identifying number, type, size, condition, location, named players, responsible adult, checkout date, and due date. At handover, the coordinator and family should confirm the condition and accessories together. Give the family a copy of the agreement with the return arrangements and a direct way to report damage or request an extension. Keep contact details available only to volunteers who need them for loan administration.

Ask the adult to confirm their preferred contact method at checkout and renewal, and send a short confirmation while there is still time to correct an error. Offer a paper or telephone route for families who use email infrequently. An alternative contact can help if the family wishes to provide one. Updating a telephone number should take one message or a conversation at rehearsal.

**Make returns easy to complete.** Send a reminder one week before the due date. Offer a staffed handback at rehearsal and a second appointment for families who cannot attend. Record the return immediately and give a receipt covering the instrument and accessories. If an appointment is missed, contact the family within two working days to agree a new date or document an extension. After a week without agreement, the coordinator should refer the case to the program lead for personal follow-up. When a delay affects a waiting player, give that family a revised update date without disclosing the borrower’s circumstances.

## Repair decisions and budget

At the average bill of 90 currency units, nine repairs would cost an estimated **810**, or 27% of the sponsorship. If all nine bills equal the average and qualify under the agreement, **2,190** would remain. The average is a planning figure. It gives no assurance about the cost or completion date of any individual job.

Authorize an initial repair allocation of up to 810 in total, once the treasurer confirms eligible spending and when funds will arrive. Obtain itemized estimates and turnaround dates before committing work. If the total exceeds 810, the treasurer should bring the revised amount and its effect on available instruments to the board for prompt approval. Hold the estimated balance for eligible costs during the year until the initial repair bills and the sponsor’s terms are clear. Exclude refundable deposits from spending plans and from income forecasts.

A teacher should flag playability concerns, and a qualified repairer should assess uncertain cases. Withdraw any instrument judged unsafe. In scheduling work, give priority to a repair that prevents a current player from losing access or releases a suitable instrument for a waiting player before rehearsals. Where two jobs would serve equally urgent needs, use quoted completion dates and costs to decide the order. Record the fault, approval, bill, and date each instrument returns to service. Encourage families to report faults promptly, and explain that ordinary wear is covered by the program. Any proposed charge for damage should receive individual review, with the family able to respond.

## Six weeks to opening rehearsal

| Timing | Action and responsibility |
|---|---|
| Week 1 | The coordinator reconciles the register against instruments in storage and contacts current borrowers. Teachers identify the instruments due for repair and any immediate playability concerns. The treasurer confirms sponsor terms and payment timing. |
| Week 2 | The coordinator checks contact details, sibling arrangements, renewal requests, and each waiting applicant’s type and size requirements. The repairer provides estimates. The treasurer authorizes eligible work within the approved allocation. |
| Week 3 | The coordinator applies the published priorities, sends confirmed offers where possible, and gives every remaining family an individual update. Teachers check proposed substitutions with the player before an offer is finalized. |
| Week 4 | Volunteers arrange returns and fittings. The coordinator checks repair progress and contacts affected families if a completion date slips. The program lead reviews unresolved shortages by type and size. |
| Week 5 | Volunteers complete handovers, record condition and accessories, and issue agreements. The coordinator follows up on unaccepted offers and gives families a clear response deadline before reallocating an instrument. |
| Week 6 | Teachers verify at the first rehearsal that each issued instrument fits and plays properly. The coordinator records who is still waiting, the reason, and the next date each family will hear from the program. |

## How the board should judge the trial

At the first-term review, report access in terms of children as well as instruments. Show how many of the original 14 applicants received a suitable instrument by the first rehearsal, how many took up a later offer, and how many still lacked one. Report new applicants separately so later demand does not obscure the opening result. Give the reasons for unfilled requests, including size mismatch, repair delay, and lack of stock. Count children sharing successfully and record cases where sharing proved impractical.

For recovery, report the number of loans due, the number returned late, the length of delays, and any instrument still outstanding. Distinguish agreed extensions from missed dates. Compare the late count with last term’s six, while recognizing that a rate comparison requires the number due in each term. For repairs, show actual spending, time out of service, and how many completed jobs put an instrument into a player’s hands. The treasurer should report sponsor funds received, spent, committed, and available.

Continue the trial through the year if difficulties can be addressed through scheduling, contact updates, or repair capacity. Bring the policy back earlier if missed returns repeatedly prevent other children from playing or if unrecovered losses threaten the program budget. Before proposing a deposit, identify the specific problem it could address, the amount families would need to provide, the waiver and refund arrangements, and the likely administrative cost. At year end, the board can then decide both whether to retain no-deposit access and how to fund repairs when the sponsorship ends.

# Instrument loan program decision paper

## Decision requested

Approve a one-year, no-deposit trial for instrument loans, starting this term. Accept the sponsor’s 3,000 currency units, subject to written confirmation of eligible expenses, and authorize repair assessments immediately. Adopt a published allocation policy and a single loan register that records sibling sharing, verified contact details, instrument condition, and return dates. Review readiness two weeks before rehearsals and review trial results at the end of each term.

The board has two distinct decisions to make. **Access policy determines which young musicians can borrow an instrument and what they must do before receiving it.** It includes deposits, waiting-list priorities, and sibling sharing. **Recovery and repair policy determines how the orchestra keeps track of instruments, gets them back on time, and returns them to playable condition.** It includes the loan register, reminders, follow-up, condition checks, and repair funding. A refundable deposit sits across both decisions. It creates an upfront requirement for families and may provide money against a charge if the agreement permits a deduction. The proposed trial removes the upfront payment while strengthening the practices that address the problems recorded last term.

## What the orchestra can plan for today

The orchestra owns 75 instruments and has 62 recorded as out on loan. That leaves 13 recorded as off loan, with 14 applicants waiting and nine instruments due for repair. The figures do not establish how many playable instruments can be offered. The repair list may include instruments still with borrowers, and the physical count may differ from the register. If all nine repairs are among the 13 off-loan instruments, only four of those 13 would be available before repairs, assuming those four are playable. If all 13 off-loan instruments are playable, they could cover at most 13 of the 14 applicants before any further returns. In either case, instrument type, size, and suitability may reduce the number of placements.

Poorly recorded sibling sharing adds another uncertainty. The count of 62 should represent individual instruments, while the register should also show every musician using each one. A family may have one instrument serving two players, and an arrangement that worked last term may no longer work if their rehearsal schedules change. The first inventory check should establish where each instrument is, who uses it, whether it is playable, and when it could next be issued.

Last term, six instruments came back late and four families had outdated contact details. The number of loans due for return is unknown, and the two groups may overlap. These counts identify two processes to improve. The orchestra should confirm contact information before issuing or renewing a loan and give families clear return dates and practical ways to meet them. It should also record how many loans are due so the board can compare late-return rates across terms.

## Access choices

A **refundable deposit** gives the orchestra funds it can hold temporarily and potentially apply against an agreed charge. Its value depends on the deposit amount, the circumstances in which deductions are permitted, and the consistency of collection and refund procedures. Even when fully refundable, it requires families to have money available at the point of borrowing. A lower amount, installments, or a confidential waiver can reduce that burden. Each adds an administrative step, and a waiver requires families to ask for an exception. If the board adopts deposits, it should approve the amount, waiver process, deduction and appeal rules, and refund timetable before applying them. Finance volunteers would need to track each family’s balance as money potentially owed back. The sponsor’s funds cannot be spent on deposits.

A **one-year no-deposit trial** lets eligible families accept a loan without an upfront payment and gives the board a full cycle of issue, renewal, and return to assess the program. Its financial trade-off is that the orchestra holds no deposit to draw on when a borrower owes an agreed charge. For the trial, use a signed agreement, an issue and return condition record, and a clear process for dealing with damage or loss. Keep ordinary wear and routine servicing within the program budget. For damage beyond ordinary wear or for loss, contact the family, review the circumstances and the documented condition, and use the orchestra’s approved terms before assessing any charge. Give families a way to ask for a review or hardship consideration. Apply the trial terms to new loans and renewals, and honor any refund terms already agreed with existing borrowers.

Allocate available instruments by teaching suitability and need. A teacher should confirm the instrument type and size each player can use. Among applicants who can use the same instrument, give priority to those without reliable access to a suitable instrument for rehearsals and practice, then use application date to break ties. Apply the same criteria to renewal requests at the scheduled review point, while honoring current loan terms. Tell families how offers are made, when they need to respond, and when they can expect another update. Give an applicant who is passed over because an instrument is unsuitable their original application date for the next suitable offer.

Keep sibling sharing available where the teacher and family confirm that both musicians can use the instrument safely and have sufficient rehearsal and practice time. Record one accountable adult, both musicians, and the agreed schedule against the same asset. Review the arrangement at renewal or when rehearsal schedules change. If sharing no longer meets one sibling’s needs, assess that player for a separate loan under the standard criteria.

## Recovery and repair choices

Assign one loan coordinator to maintain the register and a named backup to cover absences. Use one record per instrument with its asset ID, type and size, location, condition, loan status, accountable adult, registered players, verified contact information, and due date. Record repair status and expected completion dates in the same register. Limit family contact details to the people who administer loans. Teachers need access to availability, suitability, and sharing information for their pupils.

At issue or renewal, ask the responsible adult to confirm a preferred contact method, record the return or review date, and provide a copy of the agreement. Send a reminder one week before the due date. If the instrument is overdue, follow up directly within two working days and offer a practical handover time. Log any agreed extension and notify the teacher if the instrument was expected for another player. Refer unresolved cases to a designated board member after a week overdue so that further contact and any action under the agreement have a clear owner. Record receipt and inspect the instrument promptly so it can be offered again or sent for repair.

At the stated average of 90 currency units, the nine known repairs would cost about **810**, leaving **2,190** of the sponsor’s **3,000** if all nine repairs are covered and actual costs match the estimate. The 810 is a planning figure. Obtain estimates and completion dates, including any parts delays, before committing the money. Authorize the treasurer and loan coordinator to approve up to 1,000 in aggregate for the initial repairs once the sponsor confirms eligibility. If estimates exceed that amount, bring the quotes and proposed repair order to the board promptly. Keep the balance available for approved repair and maintenance during the year, subject to the sponsor’s terms. Track commitments and invoices against the grant and report the remaining balance each term.

Prioritize repairs that restore a suitable instrument for a waiting player or prevent an interruption for a current player. Use turnaround time to decide between jobs of similar urgency. For a costly repair, ask the teacher and treasurer to assess likely useful life and whether the instrument can serve an identified need before approving the work. Classify instruments with playability or safety issues as unavailable until cleared. Confirm what the grant will cover this year and use actual spending to estimate the repair budget the orchestra will need once the sponsorship ends.

## Six-week implementation

**Week 1.** Appoint the coordinator, backup, and board escalation contact. Reconcile the register with instruments in storage, loan agreements, and the repair list. Confirm the sponsor’s terms and obtain repair estimates with dates. Ask all 14 waiting applicants to confirm the instrument and size they need, whether they have another suitable instrument, and how to reach them. Confirm contact details with current borrowers whose loans are due for renewal or return.

**Weeks 2 and 3.** Send priority repairs for service and confirm which loans are continuing, ending, or shared. Ask teachers to check suitability and timetable conflicts. Make offers as soon as playable instruments and agreed handover dates are confirmed. Give each family a response deadline and contact them directly before reallocating an unanswered offer where contact difficulties are apparent.

**Week 4.** Give the board an instrument-by-instrument readiness report for remaining demand. Show confirmed placements, repairs expected before rehearsals, returns still outstanding, and unmet needs by instrument and size. If gaps remain, ask teachers to identify workable temporary arrangements, such as a supervised instrument for rehearsals or a compatible loan from a partner organization where one is available. Confirm any cost and funding source before committing. Tell affected families what they can expect for the first rehearsal and when they will next hear from the coordinator.

**Weeks 5 and 6.** Inspect repaired and returned instruments, complete fittings and handovers, and verify that each issued loan and sharing arrangement is recorded. Follow up on any remaining gaps before the first rehearsal. Keep unplaced applicants on the list with their original application dates and a named contact for updates.

## Review and proposed resolution

At the end of each term, report how many applicants received a suitable instrument by the first rehearsal, how many are still waiting by instrument and size, and how many declined an offer and why, where families choose to say. Report the number of loans due and the number returned late, how long they were overdue, unresolved loans, and contact problems. Show confirmed sibling-sharing arrangements, repair turnaround, repair costs, and grant balance. Ask families and teachers whether sharing, communication, and return arrangements worked in practice. Use aggregate figures for board reporting and keep family details in the loan register.

At year-end, review the deposit choice against both access and recovery outcomes. If delays cluster around missed reminders or difficult handovers, the board can address those causes directly. If significant loss or damage persists despite reliable records and follow-up, quantify the cost and assess how much a proposed deposit could realistically recover, what it would cost to administer, and how it would affect families’ ability to borrow. Use the experience of this trial and the known limits of last term’s records when judging changes.

**Proposed resolution.** Approve the one-year no-deposit trial, the allocation and sibling-sharing rules, and the loan administration procedures in this paper. Accept the 3,000 sponsorship subject to written confirmation of eligible spending, authorize up to 1,000 for initial eligible repairs, and require a readiness report two weeks before rehearsals, termly reports, and a year-end decision on the loan policy and repair budget.
